flashcards.question: Which security tool was primarily used during the DropVault security audit to intercept, craft, and replay HTTP requests?
How did the auditor bypass restriction checks in the File Upload Vulnerability (Lab 1)?
flashcards.answer: By spoofing the Content-Type to 'image/png' and including a PNG magic byte header in the body of a PHP file ('exploit.php').

flashcards.question: What primary risk is associated with the File Upload Vulnerability found in the DropVault application?
flashcards.answer: Remote Code Execution (RCE), which allows an attacker to execute arbitrary server-side script code.

flashcards.question: What sequence was used in the Path Traversal exploit (Lab 2) to read files outside the intended upload directory?
Why did the Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability (Lab 3) allow unauthorized access to admin files?
flashcards.answer: Because the server lacked access control verification and did not validate file ownership before returning file data.

flashcards.question: What are three recommended remediation steps for fixing the Path Traversal vulnerability?
flashcards.answer: Canonicalize all file paths, reject requests containing '../' or encoded sequences, and run the web server process with minimal filesystem permissions.

ragChunks.text: SECURITY AUDIT REPORT Application: DropVault (File System) Confidential | May 6, 2026 | dropvaultmock.vercel.app Vulnerability Assessment & Penetration Testing Target URL https://dropvaultmock.vercel.app/ Date May 6, 2026 Credentials Used user1 / password123 Classification Confidential Tool Used Burp Suite Community Edition v2026.3.2 Labs Completed 3 / 3 (All flags captured and verified) DropVault Security Audit Report | Confidential May 2026 | dropvaultmock.vercel.app Page 2 1. Objective This security audit was conducted on the DropVault file-system web application to identify and exploit

real vulnerabilities. Three vulnerabilities were successfully identified, exploited, and verified using Burp Suite Community Edition. All three lab flags were captured and confirmed through the Security Audit Submission portal. 2. Tools Used • Burp Suite Community Edition v2026.3.2 – HTTP interception, Repeater module for crafting and replaying requests. • Web Browser (Chrome 146) – Application navigation, manual testing, DevTools for cookie/session inspection. • Manual Analysis – Endpoint enumeration, parameter manipulation, and logic testing. 3. Methodology The application was accessed using

the provided credentials (user1 / password123). All HTTP traffic was proxied through Burp Suite for interception and analysis. Each vulnerability was tested by crafting specific payloads in Burp Suite's Repeater tab and observing server responses. Evidence was collected via screenshots at each stage. DropVault Security Audit Report | Confidential May 2026 | dropvaultmock.vercel.app Page 3 4. Vulnerability Analysis Only vulnerabilities confirmed through active exploitation and screenshot evidence are documented below. Three vulnerabilities were identified and all three flags were verified. Q2 –

File Upload Vulnerability (Lab 1) File Upload Vulnerability – Burp Suite Evidence (Screenshot 4) Severity HIGH – Executable file accepted by the server Endpoint POST /api/upload (multipart/form-data) Attack Performed Using Burp Suite Repeater, a PHP file named 'exploit.php' was uploaded with the Content-Type header spoofed to 'image/png'. The request body contained a PNG magic byte header followed by PHP code. The filename in the Content-Disposition header was set to 'exploit.php'. Server Response HTTP/2 200 OK — JSON body returned: { "message": "Security Alert: Executable detected!",

"filename": "exploit.php", "flag": "lab-52db-e4fc-60fd-809c", "url": "/api/view-upload?file=exploit.php" } Observation The server accepted the PHP executable despite the file extension mismatch. The internal upload URL was also exposed in the response, confirming path disclosure. Flag Captured lab-52db-e4fc-60fd-809c n Verified in Security Audit Submission portal Risk An attacker can upload malicious server-side scripts (PHP, JSP, etc.) and potentially execute arbitrary code on the server (Remote Code Execution). Remediation Validate both file extension and magic bytes (file signature)

server-side. Store uploads outside the web root. Rename files to random UUIDs. Never return internal file paths in API responses. Q7 – Insecure Direct Object Reference / IDOR (Lab 3) IDOR – File Retrieval UI Evidence (Screenshots 2 & 3) Severity HIGH – Unauthorized access to another user's private files Endpoint File Retrieval UI → internal API: /api/download?file= Attack Performed In the 'File Retrieval' input field on the DropVault dashboard, the path '../config/server_secrects.txt' was entered and the Fetch button was clicked. No authentication or ownership check was performed by the server

before returning the file contents. Server Response Console Output displayed: FILE: secret_plans.txt OWNER: admin lab-4132-2d1c-b186-9efd Observation The application returned a file owned by the 'admin' user to a regular authenticated user (user1). The filename, owner identity, and flag value were all exposed. No access control check was enforced between the requesting user and the file owner. Flag Captured lab-4132-2d1c-b186-9efd n Verified in Security Audit Submission portal DropVault Security Audit Report | Confidential May 2026 | dropvaultmock.vercel.app Page 4 Risk Any authenticated user

can access any other user's files — including admin files — simply by guessing or manipulating the file path. Confidential documents, credentials, and private data are fully exposed. Remediation Validate file ownership server-side before serving any file. Use opaque file IDs (UUIDs) instead of raw filenames. Implement access control checks: user must own the resource being requested. DropVault Security Audit Report | Confidential May 2026 | dropvaultmock.vercel.app Page 5 Q8 – Path Traversal (Lab 2) Path Traversal – Burp Suite Evidence (Screenshot 6) Severity HIGH – Arbitrary server file read

via directory traversal Endpoint GET /api/download?file=../config/server_secrets.txt HTTP/2 Attack Performed Using Burp Suite Repeater (Tab 14), a GET request was sent to /api/download?file=../config/server_secrets.txt. The '../' sequence was used to traverse outside the intended upload directory and access a server configuration file. Server Response HTTP/2 200 OK — Content-Type: text/html — Content-Length: 23 Response body: lab-1d36-a42c-1b97-01b4 Observation The server resolved the relative path traversal sequence without sanitization, returning the contents of a configuration file located

outside the web root. The response confirmed successful directory traversal with a 200 OK status. Flag Captured lab-1d36-a42c-1b97-01b4 n Verified in Security Audit Submission portal Risk An attacker can read any file on the server's filesystem that the web process has read access to — including .env files, private keys, database configs, and source code. Remediation Canonicalize all file paths and verify they fall within the allowed base directory. Reject any request containing '../' or encoded traversal sequences (%2e%2e%2f). Run the web server process with minimal filesystem permissions. 5.

Flags Summary All three flags were captured and submitted through the Security Audit Submission portal. Each flag was independently verified by the system. Lab Vulnerability Type Captured Flag Status Lab 1 File Upload Vulnerability lab-52db-e4fc-60fd-809c n VERIFIED Lab 2 Path Traversal lab-1d36-a42c-1b97-01b4 n VERIFIED Lab 3 IDOR lab-4132-2d1c-b186-9efd n VERIFIED System confirmation: "Security Audit Complete — You have successfully verified the security integrity of the DropVault infrastructure." 6. Conclusion The security audit of DropVault identified three high-severity vulnerabilities,

all of which were actively exploited and confirmed with captured flags: DropVault Security Audit Report | Confidential May 2026 | dropvaultmock.vercel.app Page 6 • File Upload Vulnerability (Lab 1): The server accepted a PHP executable disguised as an image. This creates a direct path to Remote Code Execution. • IDOR (Lab 3): The file retrieval feature returned admin-owned private files to a regular user with no ownership validation whatsoever. • Path Traversal (Lab 2): The download API resolved directory traversal sequences, granting read access to server configuration files outside the web

root. All three vulnerabilities are classified HIGH severity due to the direct impact on data confidentiality and server integrity. Immediate patching is recommended before any production deployment. A re-test should be performed after fixes are applied to confirm all vulnerabilities have been properly remediated.

notes.summary: The DropVault Security Audit Report documents a comprehensive vulnerability assessment and penetration testing process conducted on the DropVault file-system web application. Using tools like Burp Suite Community Edition and Chrome DevTools, security testers successfully identified, exploited, and verified three high-severity security vulnerabilities. These exploits resulted in the complete retrieval of authorization flags across three structured labs, confirming deep-seated flaws in the application's input handling and access control systems. Specifically, the audit uncovered a File Upload Vulnerability (Lab 1) allowing potential Remote Code Execution, an Insecure Direct Object Reference or IDOR (Lab 3) exposing administrative files to regular users, and a Path Traversal flaw (Lab 2) allowing arbitrary directory exploration and system file reads. The report highlights that all discovered vulnerabilities pose substantial threats to server integrity and data confidentiality, recommending immediate, comprehensive remediation before any production deployment.
bulletPoints: Objective: Identify and exploit real-world vulnerabilities on the DropVault file-system web application using Burp Suite Community Edition.
Lab 1 (File Upload Vulnerability): Exploded via a spoofed PHP file disguised as an image, resulting in high-severity risk of Remote Code Execution.
Lab 2 (Path Traversal): Exploded via '../' relative path manipulation, allowing arbitrary read access to sensitive system files like configuration databases.
Lab 3 (IDOR): Exploded by manipulating the file retrieval input, enabling non-admin users to fetch unauthorized admin-owned files without access control validation.
Key Remediation Strategies: Enforce strict server-side validation (magic bytes and extensions), canonicalize file paths, use opaque UUIDs, and implement robust access control checks.
notes.easyExplanation: Imagine DropVault is a digital storage warehouse. This audit found three major security flaws. First, the File Upload vulnerability is like an security guard who lets a disguised wolf into the warehouse just because it wore a sheep's mask (spoofing a PHP file as a safe PNG image). Second, the IDOR vulnerability is like a mailroom clerk handing over the boss's private mail to a regular visitor just because the visitor asked for it, without checking if they had permission. Third, Path Traversal is like a customer finding a secret staircase (using '../' commands) that lets them bypass the public reception desk to wander straight into the private management filing cabinets. To fix this, the warehouse needs strict ID checks, secure locks, and random safe deposit box names instead of raw labels.
notes.examNotes: Crucial exam focus areas: 1. Remote Code Execution (RCE) occurs when executable files (like PHP) bypass upload filters. Fix this by checking both file extensions and Magic Bytes (file signatures). 2. IDOR occurs when an application exposes internal object references without verifying ownership. Fix by implementing server-side access control lists (ACLs) and utilizing randomized UUIDs. 3. Path Traversal utilizes directory traversal characters (like '../') to read files outside the web root. Fix by canonicalizing paths and validating they belong to the permitted base directory. 4. Always validate data server-side; client-side checks can be easily bypassed using interception tools like Burp Suite.

keyDefinitions.definition: A security flaw where an application allows users to upload executable or malicious files to the server without proper type and signature validation, potentially leading to Remote Code Execution (RCE).
A vulnerability occurring when a web application exposes a direct reference to an internal implementation object (such as a database key or filename) without validating the requester's authorization.
An exploit where attackers manipulate file paths using traversal sequences (such as '../') to access restricted directories and files outside the intended web root.
The unique signature bytes at the beginning of a file used by operating systems and servers to reliably identify the actual file format, regardless of its file extension.
The process of converting path names or data representations into a standard, normalized, and unambiguous form before validation checks are applied.

subtopics.title: Audit Metadata and Methodology
items: Primary Tool: Burp Suite Community Edition v2026.3.2
Methodology: Intercepting HTTP traffic, endpoint enumeration, and crafting payloads using Burp Repeater
Overall Progress: 3 of 3 labs completed and flags captured

subtopics.title: Lab 1: File Upload Vulnerability (Q2)
items: Severity: HIGH (Risk of Remote Code Execution)
Exploitation Technique: Uploaded 'exploit.php' with Content-Type spoofed to 'image/png' and PNG magic bytes in body
Observation: Server accepted executable file and exposed internal upload path in API response
Remediation: Validate file extensions and magic bytes server-side, rename files to random UUIDs, and store uploads outside web root

subtopics.title: Lab 3: Insecure Direct Object Reference / IDOR (Q7)
items: Severity: HIGH (Unauthorized access to admin files)
Exploitation Technique: Path traversal and IDOR payload inputting '../config/server_secrects.txt' to fetch secret files
Observation: Server returned admin-owned 'secret_plans.txt' to user1 without authentication or ownership checks

flashcards.question: What is an IDOR vulnerability?
flashcards.answer: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) occurs when an application provides direct access to objects based on user-supplied input without performing proper authorization or ownership checks.

flashcards.question: What is the primary risk associated with a File Upload Vulnerability?
flashcards.answer: The potential for Remote Code Execution (RCE) by allowing an attacker to upload and execute malicious server-side scripts like PHP or JSP files.

flashcards.question: How does a Path Traversal attack function?
flashcards.answer: It uses sequences like '../' to navigate outside the intended directory structure, allowing an attacker to access sensitive configuration files or source code stored elsewhere on the server.

flashcards.question: What is the recommended remediation for Path Traversal?
flashcards.answer: Canonicalize all file paths, verify they stay within the allowed base directory, reject requests containing traversal sequences, and use minimal filesystem permissions for the web server process.

flashcards.question: Why is it dangerous to return internal file paths in API responses?
flashcards.answer: It exposes the server's directory structure, which helps attackers map the filesystem and identify locations of sensitive files for further exploitation.

flashcards.question: What is the most effective way to prevent File Upload vulnerabilities?
flashcards.answer: Validate both file extensions and magic bytes (file signatures) on the server side, rename files to random UUIDs, and store uploaded files outside of the web root.
